items.title: Supreme Court initiates suo motu case on proposed relocation of 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library
items.summary: The Supreme Court has taken suo motu cognisance of concerns surrounding the proposed relocation of the 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library (CSL) from Shastri Bhawan in New Delhi, which is slated for demolition as part of the Central Vista redevelopment project. The matter is listed for hearing on October 5 before a bench of Justices PV Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva . CSL, which functions under the Union Ministry of Culture, was established as the Imperial Secretariat Library in Calcutta in 1891. According to its website, the CSL was moved to Delhi after the capital was shifted in 1911 and has been housed at Shastri Bhawan since 1969. It is the second-largest Central government library after the National Library in Kolkata. Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva (supreme court judges) The library currently occupies around 5,500 square metres across four floors and has a collection of more than 8.5 lakh volumes, including rare books, government publications, official records and gazetteers. The Culture Ministry initially sought approximately 5,466 square metres for the library in the redeveloped Central Secretariat. Concerns over its future arose after the Directorate of Estates under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) proposed allotting two rooms, measuring around 300 square metres at Kartavya Bhawan-2, for the library. The Culture Ministry subsequently informed MoHUA in February that the proposed space was inadequate to house the library's complete collection and facilities and that complete relocation to the allotted space was not feasible. #BREAKING : Supreme Court takes suo motu cognisance of concerns over the fate and relocation of the 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library, which houses over 8.5 lakh books, amid the proposed demolition/redevelopment of Shastri Bhawan under the Central Vista project… pic.twitter.com/2U2k1QFCAc — Bar and Bench (@barandbench) October 4, 2026

items.title: ‘Ilaiyaraaja gave Dorothy a soul’: Director Karthik Subbaraj opens up about his new hit
items.summary: In the 14 years he has been in the industry, director Karthik Subbaraj has seen his audience clap for his craft and whistle along in joy. With Iraivi (2016), he received quiet smiles and some tears of appreciation too. After that came mass films, some of which left audiences suitably happy. A decade later, for his tenth film, Dorothy , which speaks of friendship between two children and what transpires after one comes out as a trans woman, Karthik has received a gift unlike any other — audiences weeping with a mixture of relief and joy, trans women thanking him for making them feel seen, and warm hugs from absolute strangers. At a press meet, some trans women thanked the director for the film and referred to him as their younger brother. Sananth and Rishikanth, the leads, have been seen wiping the tears of audience members after the end credits rolled. Every theatre visit features warm hugs and a general sense of appreciation for making Dorothy . But it did not begin this way. After Dorothy premiered at TIFF, some social media handles began a hate campaign because it speaks about LGBTQIA+ issues. Everyone seemed worried, but not Karthik. His simple mantra is “Be calm & believe in the audience.” It worked. Ilaiyaraaja’s score for the film has worked its magic. His lyrics and tune for the evocative ‘Muthumani’ have left many in tears. One trans woman said in an interview that many like her would use the song for future rituals. Karthik was in Hyderabad for the film’s Telugu release. In a more than hour-long phone interview, TNM caught up with him about why Dorothy needed to be made, what it took to make a film that crushes the male ego, and extracting amazing performances from his cast. The response to Dorothy has left many stunned. Did you expect this much love? I knew that if people watched it with an open mind, it would connect with them emotionally. I thought it might make some uncomfortable and guilty for how they treat trans people and encourage them to be compassionate instead. But I did not expect it to trigger so much conversation. It was an emotional roller coaster writing this film. I did not foresee the wave of love and the extent to which it would reach people. With each passing day, each re-watch, viewers are rejoicing in the small details they uncover. How does that make you feel? For every movie, once the storyline is in place, I begin my research. items.title: Beyond ‘cleaning’ voter rolls: The digital machinery behind SIR
items.summary: The Election Commission of India (ECI) and the Indian government have consistently framed the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) as a routine and much-needed clean-up of India’s electoral rolls. In reality, however, it marks a deep shift. The push to use software systems to sanitise electoral rolls could be traced to the early 2000s with the explosion of the Information Technology industry. Despite the massive relevance of these systems in our democracy, the ECI has publicly disclosed very little about their algorithms and software architecture. The goal is no longer maintaining unique voters in the electoral system with no duplicate records. With the SIR, the goal is also to create a tech-driven, centralised, algorithmic mapping of individuals, their networks, familial and marital ties. The technology behind SIR could pave the way for increasing centralisation and automation of electoral roll management. This raises questions about who ultimately makes decisions about inclusion and exclusion from the electoral roll, what role election officials retain, and whether the technology being used is subject to the transparency and safeguards that govern the electoral process. EROs, BLOs sidelined? At the centre of this ecosystem sits ECINET, a centralised portal that integrates all election-related services for voters and candidates, displays election results, and logs complaints related to electoral rolls. A super app, as one might call it, for all electoral functions of the ECI. Not a lot of information is available about ECINET’s functions. Instead, let us look at ERONET 2.0, a network of Electoral Registration Officers (EROs). In its annual report for 2024–25, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), which built the software, showcased ERONET 2.0 as a ‘success client’ story. It described ERONET 2.0 as the end-to-end life cycle of electors that has revolutionised electoral roll management in India. It further said, “ERONET 2.0 application has a centralised database that serves as the single source of truth for the election body.” The electoral roll is a source of truth for elections, which needs to be public. Its preparation is a democratic exercise, and requires transparency and public hearings to remove anyone from electoral rolls. All of this is governed through the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
